issues.legal_issue: Judicial acts performed within a judicial officer’s jurisdiction are protected from civil liability even when alleged to be erroneous, and an unsupported threat to sue the officer over those acts is not a bona fide lawful step.
material_facts: The judicial officer had authority to try and decide the suits in which the disputed decisions were made.
The allegations of wrongfulness, malice, and dishonesty concerned findings made in the discharge of judicial duties.
The notice threatened a damages action but gave no particulars or factual basis for the allegations.
issues.conclusion: The judicial officer’s acts were absolutely protected from civil action, and the notice could not be treated as a bona fide preliminary step to a lawful suit.
issues.legal_principle: Section 1 of the Judicial Officers’ Protection Act, 1850 protects acts done in the discharge of judicial duties within the officer’s jurisdiction absolutely, without inquiry into whether they were erroneous or done in good faith. ‘Jurisdiction’ means the officer’s general authority to act in the matter, and an error in exercising jurisdiction is not a lack of jurisdiction. For acts outside jurisdiction, the protection applies where the officer in good faith believed that jurisdiction existed. The Court relied on Anwar Hussain v. Ajoy Kumar Mukerjee & Ors.

predicates.contempt_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal from a conviction for contempt arising from a communication about a judicial officer.
predicates.judge_had_general_authority_over_the_mat: The judicial officer had general authority to hear and decide the matter in which the challenged acts occurred.
predicates.challenged_acts_were_done_in_judicial_du: The acts challenged in the threatened civil claim were performed by the officer while carrying out judicial duties.
predicates.judicial_acts_are_civilly_protected: The judicial acts are protected from civil liability.

issues.definition: When an appeal from a contempt conviction concerns a threatened civil claim over acts performed by an officer with authority over the matter, those judicial acts are civilly protected.

issues.legal_issue: An unsupported, malicious attack on a judge’s integrity and impartiality in performing judicial functions can scandalize the court and constitute criminal contempt.
material_facts: After losing suits, the appellant sent the deciding judicial officer a notice accusing the officer of inventing facts and intentionally manipulating evidence to help the opposing party.
The notice alleged bad faith, malice, partiality, and dishonesty without providing supporting particulars, and threatened a damages claim.
The notice was sent while execution proceedings and an application to stay execution were pending.
The appellant continued to defend the allegations and did not express contrition.
issues.conclusion: The notice was a deliberate attempt to scandalize and embarrass the judicial officer and lower the authority of the court, and its issuance constituted criminal contempt.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(c)(i) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 covers conduct that scandalizes or tends to scandalize, or lowers or tends to lower, a court’s authority. Section 2(c)(ii) covers conduct that prejudices or interferes or tends to interfere with the due course of a judicial proceeding. The Court held that unfounded imputations of mala fides, bias, or dishonesty against a judge, including in relation to decided matters, can undermine public confidence and amount to criminal contempt under section 2(c)(i); interference with a pending judicial proceeding can also bring conduct within section 2(c)(ii).

issues.legal_issue: The statutory protection for publications connected with non-pending proceedings does not apply to contempt that consists of scandalizing a court.
material_facts: The suits had been decided before the notice was issued, although execution proceedings and an application for a stay were pending.
The notice primarily scandalized the judicial officer by making unsupported allegations of malice, bias, and dishonesty.
The contempt finding rested primarily on the scandalizing character of the notice, rather than on interference with a pending proceeding.
issues.conclusion: The non-pending-proceeding exception did not protect the appellant because the contempt primarily fell within the category of scandalizing the court.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3(1) and (2) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 concern contempt involving interference with the course of justice in connection with a pending proceeding. Section 3(2) does not extend to contempt under section 2(c)(i), which is a distinct category. Under the explanation to section 3, a proceeding heard and finally decided is not pending merely because execution proceedings remain pending. The Court also noted that section 3 does not cover contempt otherwise different from the kinds described in section 3(1).

issues.definition: If the underlying case has been decided and the contempt consists of scandalizing the court, the non-pending-proceeding exception does not apply.

issues.legal_issue: Scandalizing a judicial officer in connection with the performance of judicial functions can substantially interfere with or tend substantially to interfere with the due course of justice and therefore be punishable.
material_facts: The appellant recklessly imputed malice and lack of good faith to the judicial officer who had decided cases against him.
The imputations were unsupported and scandalous, and the appellant did not retract them or show remorse.
The notice attacked the officer in relation to the discharge of judicial functions.
issues.conclusion: The contempt substantially interfered or tended substantially to interfere with the due course of justice and was punishable under section 13.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 prohibits imposing a sentence unless the contempt is of such a nature that it substantially interferes, or tends substantially to interfere, with the due course of justice. The Court held that scandalizing a judicial officer in relation to judicial functions satisfies that threshold because the due course of justice is a facet of the broader administration of justice.
